title: Cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS: budding yeast
vignette: A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to a week of progressive headaches and confusion. He was treated for viral esophagitis 6 months ago and Pneumocystis pneumonia 2 months ago. Temperature is 38 C (100.4 F), blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg, and pulse is 64/min. The patient is lethargic and oriented to person and place only. CT scan of the head shows a mildly increased ventricle size but no other abnormalities. Lumbar puncture reveals an elevated opening pressure, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows moderately increased protein concentration and pleocytosis. The latex agglutination test is positive for soluble polysaccharide antigen. Light microscopy of this patient's cerebrospinal fluid is most likely to reveal which of the following?

clues.text: viral esophagitis 6 months ago and Pneumocystis pneumonia 2 months ago
clues.note: Recurrent opportunistic infections (viral esophagitis, Pneumocystis pneumonia) indicate untreated AIDS (low CD4), setting up an opportunistic CNS infection.
Cryptococcal meningitis characteristically raises CSF opening pressure (from inflammation and yeast/capsular polysaccharide obstructing CSF outflow at the arachnoid villi).
A positive CSF latex agglutination for soluble POLYSACCHARIDE antigen detects the cryptococcal capsule - essentially diagnostic of Cryptococcus neoformans meningoencephalitis.

whatMatters: An AIDS patient (recurrent opportunistic infections) with subacute headache/confusion, elevated CSF opening pressure, and a positive CSF latex agglutination for soluble polysaccharide antigen has cryptococcal meningitis. Cryptococcus neoformans is a YEAST with a thick polysaccharide capsule; light microscopy of CSF shows round/oval BUDDING YEAST (narrow-based buds; India ink highlights the capsule). Answer A.
strategy: Identify the organism from the capsular polysaccharide antigen (Cryptococcus), then recall its microscopic morphology: a budding YEAST (India ink shows a halo). Answer A. Match the distractors to other fungi: germ tubes = Candida albicans; nonseptate wide-angle hyphae = Mucor/Rhizopus; spherules with endospores = Coccidioides; sporangium = mold (Rhizopus) - none are a capsule-antigen-positive yeast.

eliminations.label: Germ tubes - Candida albicans
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: C. albicans forms germ tubes when incubated in serum at 37 C. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: Candida meningitis is rare and wouldn't give a positive cryptococcal polysaccharide antigen. ✅ Correct if: identifying C. albicans (germ tube test).

eliminations.label: Nonseptate hyphae - Mucor/Rhizopus, your pick
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: Mucor and Rhizopus show broad, nonseptate hyphae branching at wide angles (mucormycosis). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: they cause rhino-orbital/sinus disease in diabetics, not a capsule-antigen-positive CSF; Cryptococcus is a yeast. ✅ Correct if: invasive sinus infection in diabetic ketoacidosis or neutropenia.

eliminations.label: Spherules with endospores - Coccidioides
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: Coccidioides immitis forms tissue spherules packed with endospores. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it usually causes community-acquired pneumonia (Southwest US); CNS disease is rare and wouldn't give a cryptococcal antigen. ✅ Correct if: pneumonia/desert exposure with spherules.

eliminations.label: Sporangium - mold (Rhizopus)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: molds like Rhizopus produce sporangia containing spores. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: Cryptococcus is a yeast and doesn't form sporangia. ✅ Correct if: a sporangium-forming mold.

reasoning: Recurrent opportunistic infections = untreated AIDS (low CD4)
Subacute meningoencephalitis with elevated CSF opening pressure
Positive CSF latex agglutination for soluble polysaccharide antigen = cryptococcal capsule
-> Cryptococcus neoformans; microscopy shows budding yeast; answer A
mechanism: Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast acquired by inhalation (soil, pigeon droppings) that causes meningoencephalitis in patients with untreated AIDS (CD4 <100/mm^3). It presents subacutely with progressive headache, fever, and confusion, and characteristically raises CSF opening pressure because inflammation and yeast/capsular polysaccharide obstruct CSF resorption at the arachnoid villi. Diagnosis is made by detecting the soluble polysaccharide (cryptococcal) antigen in CSF by latex agglutination and by visualizing the organism: round or oval BUDDING YEAST with narrow-based buds, classically demonstrated with an India ink stain that reveals a clear capsular halo. Treatment is amphotericin B plus flucytosine (induction) followed by fluconazole. The distractors correspond to Candida (germ tubes), Mucor/Rhizopus (nonseptate hyphae), Coccidioides (spherules with endospores), and sporangium-forming molds - none is a capsule-antigen-positive yeast.

difficulty.message: First Aid Micro > Cryptococcus neoformans: encapsulated budding yeast; AIDS meningoencephalitis; India ink + latex agglutination (polysaccharide antigen); high opening pressure; ampho B + flucytosine.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Nonseptate hyphae (your pick) is Mucor/Rhizopus (sinus disease in diabetics), not a capsule-antigen-positive CSF yeast; germ tubes = Candida; spherules = Coccidioides.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.message: Microscopy/India ink: round-oval yeast with a narrow-based bud and a clear capsular halo. Anchor: 'capsule antigen + halo = Cryptococcus = budding yeast.'
